title: East Siberian ice wedges recording dust transport variability during the Late Pleistocene

paper_content.abstract: During the Late Pleistocene, a severely cold and dry climate strengthened dust production across the Northern Hemisphere. Despite many studies examining aridification and dust production, there is a lack of understanding about dust transportation during global climate variability. Long-range transported (LRT) dust can be traced by comparing global geochemical signatures and constraining provenance relationships. Here we report rare earth element abundances and strontium, neodymium, and oxygen isotope compositions of inorganic substances in ice wedges from Batagay and Central Yakutia (Cyuie and Churapcha), which comprise Yedoma deposits that formed in unglaciated Beringia. Distinct geochemical properties reflect differences between local and LRT dust contributions. Particles in the Batagay ice wedges show higher similarities to Chinese aeolian deposits, while those in Central Yakutia indicate stronger local input. These provenance constraints highlight variability in atmospheric circulation transporting dust to the Arctic during the Late Pleistocene, linking climate changes to aerosol distribution.
paper_content.introduction:
Mineral dust in the atmosphere, one of the key components of the climate system, can be used as an indicator to examine climate change. It is transported by the Earth’s wind regime, affected by both the regional and large-scale climate system1. Dust in proximal regions is mainly carried by near-surface winds via creeping and saltation2,3, while long-range transport (LRT) from distal regions is largely driven by synoptic-scale atmospheric circulation3,4. The frequency and intensity of such LRT events may be modulated by millennial-scale climate oscillations5. Additionally, atmospheric dust directly absorbs and scatters radiation and indirectly modifies the properties of clouds, affecting Earth’s climate systems6,7. Dust radiative forcing also makes an important contribution to polar amplification8. Thus, investigating the provenance, distribution, and transport of dust is crucial to understanding dust-climate linkages and how atmospheric conditions respond to climate change.

During the last glacial period, dust production and deposition were greatly enhanced9,10. Dust is recorded in many deposits, particularly loess, which can incorporate both LRT dust and locally derived material9. Loess is primarily composed of silt-sized particles (2–63μm), but often incorporates a significant fraction finer than 10μm, potentially reflecting background dust transported hundreds to thousands of kilometers by westerlies11,12. Accordingly, loess and loess-like deposits serve as valuable archives of past dust dynamics. Located across central and northern Siberia, Yakutia is one of the major regions where loess is distributed11,13,14, and there is a special type of loess-like deposits called Yedoma (Fig. 1; Supplementary Fig. 1). Yedoma, or ice complex, is a silt-dominated ice-rich syngenetic permafrost with massive ice wedges, which developed across Beringia during the Late Pleistocene11,15,16. Although Yedoma in Alaska (i.e., eastern Beringia) has been considered to be aeolian-processed deposits since ref. 17, the depositional processes of Yedoma in Siberia (i.e., western Beringia) remain debated13,15,16. Because it lies at the interface between major mid-latitude dust sources and the Arctic, understanding the provenance and transport mechanisms of Yedoma source material is crucial for reconstructing past atmospheric dust circulation and its climatic implications.

Syngenetic ice wedges, widely distributed in northeastern Siberia, grew during permafrost formation and accommodated significant amounts of sediment18, recording paleoclimate and paleoenvironment conditions during permafrost development. A substantial portion of the Yedoma deposits has been lost during post-depositional permafrost degradation, changing the permafrost environment since the Pleistocene-Holocene transition19,20. Nevertheless, well-preserved syngenetic ice wedges without thaw evidence are considered to retain original materials and geochemical signatures, which were implemented during Yedoma formation21–23. To elucidate the origin and transport of Yedoma sediments during the Late Pleistocene, we sampled such well-preserved syngenetic ice wedges without any thaw-related disturbance from Batagay (upper ice complex, UIC) and Central Yakutia (Cyuie and Churapcha) (Supplementary Notes; Supplementary Figs. 2, 3; Supplementary Table 1). Formation ages of the ice wedges studied in the middle part of the Batagay UIC (~60–27 ka; ref. 24) fall within the middle to late (mid-late) Marine Isotope Stages (MIS) 3 (~45–30 ka), based on newly available radiocarbon ages (see Methods; Supplementary Notes; Supplementary Table 2), which corresponds to the period before the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM). In contrast, the Central Yakutia ice wedges formed in early to middle MIS 2 (~21–18 ka; refs. 21, 22), representing the LGM period.

In this study, we constrain the provenance and transport pathways of inorganic solid particles preserved in syngenetic ice wedges from Batagay and Central Yakutia by measuring trace element concentrations, particularly rare earth elements (REE), and isotope compositions of Sr, Nd, and O, which have been widely used to trace provenances for various types of materials (e.g., rock, sediment, and dust; refs. 1, 25–27). Formed mainly by snow compaction and hoarfrost accretion22,23, rather than surface water infiltration, our ice wedge samples effectively trap atmospheric input and are expected to preserve atmospheric dust signals. Unlike host sediments, well-preserved ice wedge infill is less affected by redeposition and sediment reworking, and thus can more directly record atmospheric deposition during ice wedge growth. Together, these datasets allow us to evaluate the relative contributions of local versus LRT sources during the mid-late MIS 3 (Batagay) and the LGM (MIS 2; Central Yakutia).
paper_content.results:
Grain-size distributions and trace element systematics
The possibility of containing the LRT dust in both regions is suggested by the bimodal to polymodal grain-size distributions, indicative of a polygenetic origin (Supplementary Notes; Supplementary Fig. 4; Supplementary Data 1; refs. 12, 28). Alongside a dominant silt-sized peak (10–80μm range), all samples display a secondary mode or shoulder around 1μm, consistent with the fine-grained LRT dust. Because REE, Sr isotope, and quartz oxygen isotope compositions can be grain-size dependent25,26,29, we therefore analyze size-separated fractions (see Methods).

REE concentrations varied across grain-size fractions but did not exhibit any systematic correlation with particle size (Supplementary Fig. 5; Supplementary Data 2). Differences between sample groups are more prominent than those among grain-size fractions, indicating that the REE concentrations are mainly controlled by provenance rather than grain-size effects. To compare the geochemical compositions of all samples and possible source areas (PSAs), Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 6 present selected element ratios, including REE and other trace elements. These data are normalized to post-Archean Australian shale (PAAS; ref. 30). The element ratios used in these binary plots have been suggested as useful particle size-independent provenance tracers25.

The binary plots suggest that our samples represent mixtures of LRT dust from the Chinese sources and locally derived material, with varying proportions (Fig. 2; Supplementary Fig. 6). The Batagay samples overlap closely with the Ordos Plateau (OP) field, suggesting a relatively stronger input from Chinese dust. In contrast, the Central Yakutia samples fall between the fields of the Lena and Yana River suspended particulate matter (SPM) and the northern China aeolian deposits, probably the OP, suggesting a mixture of regional input and distal dust sources. Europium anomalies (Eu/Eu*) also distinguish the two groups (Supplementary Notes; Supplementary Fig. 5): the Batagay samples overlap with the OP to the northern margin of the Tibetan Plateau (NMTP) fields, whereas the Central Yakutia samples align more closely with the Lena and Yana SPM (Fig. 2c, d; Supplementary Fig. 6a–e). In detail, the Lena River SPM systematically shifts toward the Aldan Shield lamproites across all element ratios. The Central Yakutia samples show a similar deviation, trending toward both the Lena River SPM and the Aldan Shield lamproites, likely demonstrating a substantial contribution from this crystalline lithology of the Aldan Shield.

Strontium and neodymium isotopes
The measured 87Sr/86Sr ratios of bulk ice wedge sediments range from 0.715784 to 0.717100 in Batagay and from 0.716610 to 0.717291 in Central Yakutia (Fig. 3; Supplementary Data 3). The fine fractions (<10 and <5μm) show higher ratios, ranging from 0.719567 to 0.722099 in Batagay and from 0.720124 to 0.721181 in Central Yakutia, indicating a grain-size effect with increasing 87Sr/86Sr toward the fine fractions. In contrast, εNd(0) values show little evidence of grain-size effects but display clear regional differences. Bulk εNd(0) values from the Batagay samples (−8.8 to −8.5) are higher than those from the Central Yakutia samples (−18.3 to −16.3), and the fine fractions show the same contrast (−8.2 to −7.9 in Batagay and −14.7 to −14.3 in Central Yakutia), highlighting the distinct provenance signals between the two sites.

The Batagay values appear near the isotope range of the Greenland glacial dust and are plotted between the ranges of Mongolian Gobi Desert (MG), northern boundary of China (NBC), Chinese Loess Plateau (CLP), and the NMTP (Fig. 3). This similarity in radiogenic isotopes suggests that our samples may share a common East Asian provenance with the Greenland glacial dust. Numerous studies have reported that dust in the Greenland ice cores originated from major dust-emitting sources in East Asia (e.g., CLP, MG, and the Taklimakan Desert, TK) during the last glacial period31–33. Although dust of European origin has also been reported in Greenland, and Sr-Nd isotopes alone are insufficient to distinguish between European and Asian sources34, geographical distance makes it more plausible that atmospheric dust deposited in our study area originated from East Asia.

Bulk Central Yakutia samples overlap with the isotopic range of Alaskan loess, and the εNd(0) values overlap with those of Aldan Shield lamproites (Fig. 3). Although direct comparison of Sr isotopes is complicated by grain-size effects and by the use of whole-rock lamproite values26,35, the εNd(0) overlap suggests a contribution from the Aldan Shield-derived material. The more radiogenic 87Sr/86Sr in the Central Yakutia samples relative to the lamproites can be attributed to grain-size partitioning26. However, the fine fractions (<10 and <5μm) shift for both Sr and Nd isotopes toward the fields of the Eastern Qinling Mountains (EQLM) and OP, suggesting additional contributions of Chinese dust, consistent with mixing signatures inferred from REE ratios (Fig. 2).

Although the reported 87Sr/86Sr values for the Lena and Yana River SPM (0.716624 to 0.717728 for the Lena; 0.713647 to 0.716892 for the Yana and its tributary; ref. 36) are similar to those of our samples, Nd isotopes for these rivers are scarce. We alternatively compare our dataset with the Laptev Sea sediments (LSS) and northeastern (NE) Siberian loess as more integrative local references (Fig. 3). The LSS cannot be regarded as a single definitive local endmember, because the LSS represents a mixture of sediments derived from diverse sources, including coastal erosion and river discharge, and because riverine SPM draining limited watersheds can have different chemical compositions37,38. Nonetheless, the isotopic similarity between LSS and all samples suggests that local sources likely contributed to the ice wedge sediments. Similarly, NE Siberian loess exhibits Sr isotopes comparable to our samples at equivalent size fractions (<5μm). However, NE Siberian loess shows Nd isotope compositions distinct from the samples. This εNd(0) discrepancy indicates that the Nd systematics require additional components, consistent with mixing between local lithologies and LRT dust. Indeed, all samples fall within the mixing field defined by several PSAs (Fig. 3b). The Batagay samples cannot be explained solely by local lithologies such as the Kharaulakh-Suordakh volcanic rocks or Aldan Shield lamproites. Because those reference values are based on whole-rock measurements and therefore not directly comparable to the fine sediment fractions, we treat them as bounding constraints on the local compositional range. The Batagay values are consistent with mixing between a set of hypothetical local endmembers (reflecting Kharaulakh-Suordakh and Aldan Shield contributions) and the OP-NMTP mixing endmembers (red dotted lines in Fig. 3b). For Central Yakutia, mixing trajectories between the OP-NMTP mixing endmembers and a local endmember defined by the bulk samples can explain the observed shift toward finer fractions (blue dotted lines in Fig. 3b). The bulk Central Yakutia compositions are taken as an approximation of the local source, showing Aldan Shield-like εNd(0) values and elevated 87Sr/86Sr compared to lamproites. Taken together, these results suggest that both study sites may contain LRT dust from the OP and NMTP in addition to local material. This interpretation is broadly consistent with the REE-based evidence (Fig. 2), which also points to contributions from Chinese PSAs. We note, however, that REE and Sr-Nd isotope signatures can be influenced by distinct grain-size and mineralogical fractions, which may account for the minor discrepancies observed between the two provenance signals. The REE data suggest OP as the dominant source (Fig. 2), whereas the Sr-Nd isotopes imply mixing with additional components (Fig. 3).

Quartz oxygen isotopes
Oxygen isotope compositions of quartz grains are effective in differentiating distinct provenances in well-mixed aeolian dust1. Since δ18O values of aeolian quartz are influenced by grain-size effects with low-temperature microcrystalline quartz29, we report grain-by-grain isotopic compositions subdivided by grain-size to avoid such effects (see Methods; Fig. 4; Supplementary Data 4). The δ18O (vs V-SMOW) distributions of all grain-size fractions are generally characterized by two dominant isotope ranges, around +10‰ and +15‰ (Fig. 4). The overall distributions differ between Batagay and Central Yakutia, and these differences are confirmed by statistical analyses (see Fig. 4 caption). For three coarser fractions (>32μm), the Batagay samples show relatively wide peak areas from +10 to +20‰, while the Central Yakutia samples have primary peaks at +10‰ and secondary peaks around +15‰. The finest fractions (<32µm) exhibit broad distributions at all sites, suggesting the mixing of various grain provenances. In particular, the dominant peak areas for the finest fraction of the Batagay samples shift toward values around +15‰, indicating distinct source contributions compared with the Central Yakutia samples.

The main +10‰ peaks of the measured δ18O values in Fig. 4 are attributed to the local influx of granitic or metamorphic components. The Batagay sampling site is located in the Yana River basin along the Verkhoyansk Range, where granitoid intrusions are common in the central part of the Verkhoyansk-Kolyma orogen (Supplementary Fig. 1; ref. 39). Through glacial erosion or river discharge, sediments from the Verkhoyansk Mountains could contain significant amounts of quartz grains with δ18O values of approximately +10‰, which may have been generated by weathering of granitoid intrusions. Similarly, in the Lena and Aldan River basins, where the Cyuie and Churapcha sampling sites are located, glaciogenic sediments and morainic materials from the Verkhoyansk Mountains during the Pleistocene are common40. Besides, the Lena River flows from the southern part of the Siberian Platform consisting of Proterozoic metamorphic rocks and granitoids41, and the Aldan River originates in the Aldan Shield which comprises Archaean metamorphic series40. Therefore, the primary sources of Lena and Aldan Rivers are crystalline rocks of metamorphic origins, may comprising the δ18O values of +10‰, which is also consistent with the radiogenic 87Sr/86Sr and εNd(0) signatures observed in the Central Yakutia samples.

The different peaks of δ18O values in the sedimentary component range of approximately +15‰ seen in Fig. 4 could be contributed by both local sources and LRT dust. The basement of central and northern Yakutia is mostly Mesozoic sedimentary rocks and Late Paleozoic and Mesozoic folded sediments, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 1; ref. 40). Either glacial erosion of local bedrock or aeolian transport like saltation from local sediments can provide a basis for δ18O values near +15‰. The sedimentary components also likely contain LRT quartz from the Chinese arid regions, as previously suggested by REE and Sr-Nd isotope systematics. In this regard, the ranges of δ18O values taking into account particle sizes from the MG (+15.1 to 17.3‰ for <16µm; +12.6 to 15.1‰ for 16−63µm) and the OP and NMTP (+16.1 to 18.5‰ for <16µm; +14.0 to 17.0‰ for 16−63µm) as reported in ref. 27 overlap with the range in which peaks for sedimentary components appear in the samples. Notably, the δ18O distribution of the Batagay samples has a prominent peak in this range (Fig. 4), suggesting that LRT dust may have contributed particularly significantly from the Chinese arid regions to Batagay during the mid-late MIS 3. In addition, for the Batagay samples, the dominant δ18O peak near +15‰ is more pronounced in the finer fractions of quartz particles than in the coarser fractions (Fig. 4d). This may reflect a larger proportion of LRT dust in the finer fractions. The contrasting proportions of +15‰ peaks between the Batagay and Central Yakutia samples likely reflect different contributions of LRT versus local material, with the Batagay distribution showing a stronger LRT component and the Central Yakutia distributions retaining more local input, consistent with the stronger local signatures in the Central Yakutia samples inferred from REE ratios (Fig. 2) and Sr-Nd isotopes (Fig. 3).
paper_content.methods:
Pretreatment
Bulk ice wedge samples were melted and oven-dried at about 40°C to extract only sediment fractions. The extracted sediment samples were sequentially pretreated with 1M HCl and 17.5% H2O2 to remove acid-soluble minerals (e.g., carbonates) and organic matter, respectively. After the sample settled from the suspension, the supernatant was removed by pipette and 17.5% H2O2 solution was added again until all organic material was removed. The resulting inorganic residue was rinsed three times with Milli-Q water and oven-dried at approximately 60°C. Each sample was divided into four portions for analyses of particle size distribution, trace elements, and radiogenic and oxygen isotopes.

Grain-size distribution
After removing acid-soluble minerals and organic materials, samples were dispersed in distilled water for particle size analysis. Measurements were performed using Mastersizer 3000 Particle Size Analyzer (Malvern Panalytical) at the Cooperative Laboratory Center, Pukyong National University, Republic of Korea. Based on laser diffraction technique, this instrument has a measurement range of 0.01 to 3500µm with 100 size classes. The grain-size distributions were calculated by the Mie scattering theory.

Trace element analyses
Trace element concentrations were analyzed for several grain-size fractions (bulk, <125μm, 63−125μm, <63μm, 32−63μm, and <32μm) obtained by dry sieving, when sufficient sample material was available. Approximately 0.1 g of each sample was weighed and dissolved in a mixture of 5 ml HF, 4 ml HNO3, and 1 ml HClO4 in Teflon digestion vessels at 185°C for 24 h. After complete dissolution, the decomposed samples were evaporated to dryness on a hot plate, re-dissolved in 3% HNO3, and diluted appropriately depending on the target elements. REE and trace element concentrations were determined using an iCAP Q (Thermo Fisher Scientific) inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (ICP-MS) at the Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST), Republic of Korea. Two certified reference materials (CRMs) MESS-4 (marine sediment) and BCR-667 (estuarine sediment) were analyzed alongside the samples to validate the accuracy. The results for the CRMs are summarized in Supplementary Table 3. For MESS-4, recoveries of certified elements are within 11% of the certified values, with relative standard deviations (RSDs) below 8.2%. For BCR-667, recoveries of certified elements are within 8.9% of the certified values, with RSDs below 1.9%.

Sr and Nd isotope analyses
Sr and Nd isotope analyses were conducted on nine bulk samples, three <10µm fractions, and three <5µm fractions using a TRITON plus (Thermo Fisher Scientific) thermal ionization mass spectrometer (TIMS) at Korea Polar Research Institute (KOPRI), Republic of Korea. The <10µm and <5µm fractions were separated by gravity sedimentation based on Stokes’ Law and subsequently recovered by centrifugation. Approximately 30 mg of each sample was dissolved in a mixture of 2 ml HF, 1 ml HNO3 and 0.1 ml HClO4 in closed Teflon vials at 120°C for 3 to 4 days. Sr was separated using quartz columns (AG 50W-X8, #100-200) with 2.5 N HCl and 6 N HCl and then loaded onto Re filaments with 1M H3PO4. Nd was extracted by quartz columns (AG 50W-X8, #200-400) using DIW and 0.2 M HIBA (α-Hydroxyisobutyric acid) solution, and loaded onto Re filaments with 0.1M H3PO4. For the bulk samples, procedural blanks were <110 pg for Sr and <60 pg for Nd. Reproducibility and accuracy were assessed by analyzing the international reference materials NBS-987 for Sr and JNdi-1 for Nd, which were treated as unknowns. Long-term measurements yielded mean values of 87Sr/86Sr = 0.710256 ± 0.000006 (2σ, n=15) for NBS-987 and 143Nd/144Nd = 0.512122 ± 0.000005 (2σ, n=15) for JNdi-1. Mass fractionation during measurement was corrected by internal normalization to 86Sr/88Sr = 0.1194 and 146Nd/144Nd = 0.7219, respectively. During the analyses of fine fractions (<10 and <5μm), procedural blanks were <41 pg for Sr and <43 pg for Nd. Repeated measurements yielded mean values of 87Sr/86Sr = 0.710252 ± 0.000006 (2σ, n=8) for NBS-987 and 143Nd/144Nd = 0.512119 ± 0.000004 (2σ, n=8) for JNdi-1. Each Sr analysis consisted of 100 measurement cycles per run, and each Nd analysis consisted of 140 cycles per run.

Oxygen isotope analysis for quartz
To measure oxygen isotopic composition of quartz grains, the samples reacted with a mixture of concentrated H2SiF6 and 10% HCl until all clay mineral was removed and only quartz grains remained. Each sample was divided into four size fractions (>125, 63−125, 32−63 and <32µm) by dry sieving. Quartz grains of >125, 63−125 and 32−63µm fractions were individually hand-picked, mounted in 1-inch epoxy and polished. Due to difficulties in sample preparation, one representative sample from each site was selected to measure the finest fractions. The finest fractions (<32μm) were mounted in 6-mm diameter acrylic resin to achieve greater flatness during polishing. NBS-28 standards were also prepared with 6-mm diameter resin mount in the same way. The polished acrylic resin mounts were embedded in an indium-filled 1-inch Al disc for higher electrical conductivity. The sample and standard mounts were embedded in the same disc, allowing measurement in the same session. All sample mounts were finally coated with gold prior to measurements.

Oxygen isotope compositions of individual quartz grains were determined by a CAMECA IMS 1300-HR3 multicollector-equipped ion microprobe at Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI), Republic of Korea. For the analysis of the coarser grains (>32µm), a 20 μm Cs+ primary beam of 2.5 to 3.0 nA accelerated at 10 kV. A 10 keV electron gun of 150 μm in diameter was applied for electrostatic charge compensation. Negative secondary ions were extracted with a potential of −10 kV. The field aperture size was 3000×3000μm. A mass resolving power (MRP) was ~5000 at 10% peak height. Both 16O and 18O were simultaneously collected in two Faraday cup detectors fitted with 1010 Ω (L’2) and 1011 Ω (H’2) resistors, respectively. Each analysis consisted of pre-sputtering (80 to 100 s), automatic beam centering to the field and contrast apertures, mass calibration for 16O, and measurements (20 cycles of 4 s). The instrumental mass fractionation (IMF) was corrected using NBS-28 quartz (δ18O V-SMOW = 9.6‰). Under these conditions, the 16O- count rate was typically ~1×109 cps/nA. An internal precision (standard error of the mean of the cycles in a single measurement; 2σ) of ±0.1 to 0.2‰ is achieved by NBS-28 quartz standards. The external reproducibility (standard deviation between several spots) was about ±0.3‰.

The finest fractions (<32µm) were also measured by in-situ spot analysis, with a 5 μm Cs+ beam of ~100 pA. 16O and 18O were detected with a Faraday cup and electron multiplier, respectively. Each analysis consisted of pre-sputtering (80 to 100 s), automatic beam centering, mass calibration, and measurements (20 cycles of 4 s). Other instrumental operation parameters were the same as the analyses of the three coarser fractions (>32µm). Under these conditions, the 16O- count rate was typically ~1×108 cps/nA. The internal precision (2σ) was ±0.3 to 0.4‰ by NBS-28 quartz standards. The external reproducibility was about ±0.4‰.

Radiocarbon age dating
After melting of ice wedge samples, we freeze-dried the samples and screened the sediments originally included in the wedge ice using a stereomicroscope. Organic macro remains were picked. Radiocarbon dating was performed at the MICADAS facility at Alfred Wegener Institute (AWI) Bremerhaven, Germany53. Plant remains were cleaned with acid-base-acid treatment as described in ref. 53. The samples were subsequently combusted in an elemental analyzer (Elementar vario Isotope). Produced CO2 was further graphitized utilizing the automated graphitization system (AGE-3; Ionplus AG; ref. 54) and radiocarbon measurements were conducted. Radiocarbon data were normalized and blank corrected against size-matched standard (NIST Oxalic Acid II, NIST SRM 4990C) and 14C-free blank material (Phthalic Acid; Sigma Aldrich 320064), and data integrity was checked against the processing wood standard IAEA-C5 and lab-internal sediment standards.

All radiocarbon results were reported as F14C and conventional radiocarbon ages (Supplementary Table 2). We used the IntCal20 dataset (ref. 55) to calibrate the ages with CALIB Radiocarbon Calibration version 8.2 (ref. 56), which are given as calibrated years before present (cal yr BP). We also calibrated non-finite ages for comparative reasons. To provide a minimum age estimate, a theoretical standard deviation of 1000 radiocarbon years was computed in CALIB following ref. 57. We have rounded all results with standard deviations in the radiocarbon ages greater than 50 yr to the nearest 10 yr.

Calculation for Sr-Nd mixing curves
Binary mixing trajectories in Fig. 3 between PSA endmembers were calculated using average Sr and Nd isotope ratios and elemental concentrations of the respective endmembers. The mixed isotopic ratio Rmix was obtained as:

Rmix = (fA CA RA + fB CB RB) / (fA CA + fB CB) (1)

where R is the isotope ratio, C is the element concentration (Sr or Nd), and f is the mixing fraction of endmembers A and B.

Oxygen isotope distributions
The δ18O distributions of quartz grains were evaluated using Gaussian kernel density estimation (KDE) with bandwidth h determined by the normal reference rule (h=σ·(4/(3n))1/5), where σ is the standard deviation and n is the number of measurements; ref. 58). KDEs were calculated using Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Ltd., USA) with the Real Statistics Resource Pack (Release 8.9.1; ref. 59). Group differences were assessed for each size fraction (>125, 63−125, 32−63, and <32µm) using three statistical approaches: Welch t-test, Mann–Whitney U test, and permutation test.

Ice-sheet reconstructions
To illustrate the ice-sheet extent in Fig. 1, we used published reconstructions of the Eurasian Ice Sheet Complex (EISC), Greenland Ice Sheet (GIS), Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS), and Cordilleran Ice Sheet (CIS) from refs. 60, 61. Within the MIS 3 reconstructions, only the 40 ka time slice shows a more extensive ice cover in eastern Siberia because it incorporates a maximum Quaternary ice-extent template to match empirical evidence from the Kamchatka Peninsula60. This likely overestimates the ice extent in the Verkhoyansk region, where field evidence indicates limited local glaciation62–64. To avoid misinterpretation, the 40 ka reconstruction was excluded, and the MIS 3 ice extent is illustrated using the 30, 35, and 45 ka time slices.

Data availability
All data generated in this study are provided in the Supplementary Information and the Source Data files.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The paper by Kim et al. deals with the dust production and the routes of long-range transported (LRT) dust be jet streams during the Late Pleistocene in the Northern Hemisphere. The study reconstructed and compared the chemical properties of dust particles worldwide and from two Yedoma sites with ice wedges in eastern Siberia (Batagay and Central Yakutia) by measuring rare earth element (REE) abundances, strontium, neodymium, and oxygen isotope compositions of inorganic substances.
The authors concluded that the Batagay and Central Yakutia samples have different geochemical properties due to differences in local and LRT mechanisms. The Batagay ice wedges show higher similarities to Chinese aeolian deposits and Greenland glacial dust while the Central Yakutia ice wedges are more representative of local materials.
This is a valuable contribution to the international community. It can be published after major revisions.
1) First, it should be clarified what is loess (or loess-like sediments) in the Yedoma formations and what is long-range transport (LRT) of dust. Both should have different grain sizes. The loess-like deposits of the so-called Yedoma consist of s silt-sized particles, but the LRT dust contains mostly smaller particles. Quartz and also coarse grained sized particles may also be local material or even recycled from older material in the area. The trapping of dust (and silt), for example by vegetation or biocrusts is also an important factor in the development of loess landscapes. Some of the material may have been temporarily deposited and then transported again. There may also be some fluvial or colluvial input to the sections. However, some signals in REE or Sr isotopes are obvious for LRT.
2) The chronological framework is very important for this study and its conclusions, and in my opinion, this needs to be improved. The authors have separated pre- and late Glacial Maximum for the Batagay and Yakutia ice wedges - but the chronological framework is quite uncertain, and not described in detail. For example, Murton et al. (2022) show quite a lot of uncertainty in the dating.
3) There is a local ice cap on the Verkhoyansk Mountains between Batagay and Central Yakutia that is out of phase with the global Last Glacial Maximum. This is also true for Pleistocene ice extent in Alaska, see e.g. Stauch and Gualtier (1–3). They have a maximum extent in MIS 4 or even just before. This shows that humidity is the main driver of ice and that local ice caps can also influence at least the local wind fields.
In addition, there were so many climatic fluctuations during the last glacial cycle that this should be clarified before drawing a big picture from the Chinese desert to Greenland based on such a rough chronological framework. For example, the aforementioned LRT of dust from China to Siberia needs to be proven and the period in which this direction occurred needs to be established. Without a time frame, the conclusion remains highly speculative. Provide some age constraints for your samples and also from the surround areas.
In my opinion, this should be also confirmed by paleoclimatic models. The North Atlantic and the distribution of the Pleistocene ice influenced the jet stream. There are local wind fields over the ice sheets, and there were easterly winds in front of the ice caps. There are quite a lot of climatic fluctuations during the last glacial cycle and therefore quite a lot of fluctuations in the direction of the jet stream. The Feno-Scandinavian ice sheet is important for the climate in Asia. In particular, during the global Last Glacial Maximum, this ice sheet, at its largest extent, blocked moist air masses to the east during its largest extent. There are eastly winds in front of the ice sheet which are also responsible for the dust and loess distribution, please see the model of Schaffernicht et al. (4), who also discussed the dust distribution in front of the European ice sheet during the LGM. Local ice can also have an influence on wind direction and especially on the transport of silt-size particles, as shown in many papers.
4) Statistics:
The biplots in Figures 2 and 3 show only the overlap between the REE or isotope ratios of the samples with those of the other proxies. In order to provide a more reliable distinction, a statistical analysis with respect to the differences between samples and proxies can improve the interpretation to which group the samples are assigned. The manuscript "East Siberian ice wedges recording the polar jet stream during the Late Pleistocene" by Kim et al. studies the provenance of mineral dust in the Late Pleistocene ice wedges collected from Siberia.
My report is very short, as I find the manuscript well structured, easy to follow, and the results and conclusions well justified. I think the manuscript is suitable for publication and would be of interest to many. I only have a few notes and corrections for the authors below.
Key results: The results indicate a significant contribution from distant Asian sources for the pre-LGM dust in the Siberian ice wedges, while the late LGM dust is more locally sourced. The authors attribute these differences to changes in the polar jet stream pathway patterns that themselves are linked to changes in the extent of ice sheets.
Validity:
The manuscript uses multiple methods to infer the provenance of the dust, making the provenance analysis more robust.
The data obtained by different methods are mostly consistent with each other and point to the conclusions presented in the manuscript. The data are also consistent with previous studies, and the compilation of data from previous studies is extensive.
Significance:
I think the results of this study are significant, not only because of the samples, which may be unavailable in the future if they melt, but also because the results offer important new insights to the links between dust and climate and will be of interest to many in the fields of dust and paleoclimate research and beyond.
Data and methodology:
Only the ICP-MS/AES methods need more details on the analytical parameters and information on the standards used.
The Sm values of the Lena and Yana SPM samples seem to be incorrectly reported in Supplementary Table 2. Please correct.
Analytical approach:
While a PCA may have been useful in presenting the REE/trace element data in a more robust way, I do not think it is absolutely necessary, since the main features are already evident from the existing figures.
I would, however, have liked to see more plots on different trace elements (possibly in the supplementary information), for example Eu/Eu*, Y/∑REE, Y/Tb, Y/La, as these are also used by the cited paper of Ferrat et al. (2011).
Suggested improvements:
Fig. 3. The grain size fraction that each dataset represents would be good to include in the figure, as the Sr isotopes can be influenced by the grain size. I would also like to hear what are the authors’ thoughts on why the Batagay values are not close to OP or EQLM if they are the main sources based on REE (Fig.2)?
While I do not disagree with the conclusions, the similarity of Greenlandic and Alaskan dust to the samples of this study are only based on the Sr-Nd isotopes. For this reason, I would add a bit of uncertainty to the conclusions about these regions. Especially since in Greenland, the Sr-Nd isotopes have not been enough to discriminate the European and Asian dust (Ujvari et al. 2015 – cited in the manuscript).
Lines 225-227: It would be nice to explain in a bit more detail why the jet stream responses to the ice sheet changes in the way that is suggested (for those who are not familiar with the atmospheric aspects of the study). So what are the mechanisms behind the changes in the jet stream pathways?
Clarity and context: The manuscript is well structured and clearly presented.

My expertise: I am not very familiar with Yedoma or permafrost deposits in general (have not worked with those).

Review of Kim et al Nature Communications
April 2025
Kim and coauthors present geochemical provenance data on Yedoma sediments from two sites in Siberia. The data include Sr-Nd isotopes and REE, presumably on the bulk fraction, and O isotopes on individual quartz grains split into several size fractions. The data are used to reconstruct the position of the northern branch of the polar jet during the LGM.
The writing is clear and the paper is well-organized with nice-looking figures. Overall, the ice wedges represent an interesting paleoclimate archive that deserves exploration. However, we have some serious concerns with the data and their interpretation, and do not consider the conclusions to be supported by the data.
Regarding the provenance data, the paper lacks sufficient characterization of the local source area geochemistry, particularly for Nd. The Laptev Sea sediments (LSS) that the authors use in place of local sediment compositions actually plot between the Batagay and Central Yakutia sites, suggesting that the LSS may reflect mixing of local materials that are simply not represented in Fig. 3. Without true characterization of the Beringia potential dust source composition, it is not possible to estimate the inputs of local vs LRT dust from Chinese deserts.
Further, we are not convinced that the sites, particularly Central Yakutia, are receiving dust from Chinese deserts. If they were, we would expect to see compositions that reflect mixing of local and long-range-transported (LRT) end-members. Instead, the Sr-Nd isotope compositions of the sites are both tightly clustered, which is more indicative of input from a single source. It’s possible that the Batagay samples follow a mixing trend between two end-members, with one of them being Chinese desert material. However, the blue points in Fig. 3 really do not appear to be following a mixing trend. Certainly if transport were occurring from Chinese deserts over both sites and onward to Greenland, the data points should follow the same mixing curve – which they clearly do not.
In addition, there are several important analytical details that are missing. One is the size distribution of the Yedoma silts used for Sr-Nd analysis. Sr isotopes are known to have a grain size effect (e.g. Biscaye and Dasch, 1971; Grousset and Biscaye, 2005; Gaiero, 2007); thus, it is important to compare apples-to-apples size fractions among different studies. In the case of LRT dust, scientists typically analyze the fine fraction (<5 um). At the very least, even if the <5 um fraction was not isolated in this study, the measured grain size fraction used for the isotope analyses needs to be stated. Based on Extended Data Fig. 5, it appears that the silts are quite coarse (10s to 100s of µm diameter) – so isotopic analysis of the bulk size fraction is not directly comparable to other fine-fraction data such as the dust from Greenland ice cores.
The Sr and Nd isotopes were run with isotopic reference materials but it is unclear whether they were used both as bracketing standards to correct the isotope ratios and as ‘unknowns’ to assess accuracy of the analyses. Given the numbers analyzed for NBS-987 (n = 100) and JNdi-1 (n = 140), it seems as though these are bracketing standards – in which case, additional reference materials should be reported to provide an independent check on the accuracy of the isotope ratios.
In addition to source area geochemistry, the inference that Beringia was a source of high-latitude dust in the past would be supported better through some mapped deposits of potential source sediments. What is the geomorphic evidence for dust generation in this region? Are there maps of glacial extent? Outwash plains?
The quartz O isotope data are interesting, in that several of the curves are bimodal, suggesting inputs from multiple sources. The interpretation related to these data would be strengthened by inclusion of comparable data on the potential source regions (e.g. Beringia and Asian deserts) included in the figure, rather than just in the text. Ideally these would be plotted against another provenance tracer (e.g. bivariate plot) and be supported by mixing calculations. The interpretation provided on Line 175 – that both >32 and <32 sediments are contributed by LRT of Chinese dust – is implausible. Considering that local sources can account for the oxygen isotope values in the coarser fraction (Line 160), it does not make sense that all this relatively coarse silt would have come thousands of km from China rather than from local sediments. We think in this case, the most parsimonious interpretation needs to be made rather than basing the interpretation on rare exceptions in the literature of long-distance coarse particle transport.
Likewise, the REE data in Extended Data Figure 4 are a helpful addition, but could be leveraged toward the interpretation more effectively by including a panel that directly compares the patterns of the different regions. We would advocate for further normalizing samples to a single element, e.g. Yb or Lu, to more effectively compare the patterns. By eyeball, the data in panels a and b actually look more similar to panel d than to panel c, supporting a local source for the Yedoma silts. Figure 2 in the main text helps with these comparisons, but we are not convinced that the Lena and Yana sediments fully characterize the local dust source region, given the older bedrock to the south, shown in Extended Data Figure 1, which would provide sediment with more negative εNd values, as shown by the Central Yakutia sites in Fig. 3.
Regarding the potential source regions shown on Fig. 3, the African sources are not relevant based on geography and atmospheric transport patterns. We would recommend removing them from the figure and discussion. In addition, the “Alaska” field reflects only the Fairbanks loess data of Biscaye et al. 1997 and not more recent data from southcentral Alaska that characterize the active Copper River dust source and related glaciofluvial sources (Koffman et al., 2022). It may be worth including these data for a more complete representation of Alaska sources.
Finally, while a Chinese desert source *could* be a plausible end-member for Batagay dust, it does not follow that the jet itself had to have gone directly over the site. There is plenty of dust transport that occurs not in the jet, for example through synoptic-scale systems. For instance, extratropical cyclones transport dust from Patagonia to Antarctica, including onto the East Antarctic plateau – yet the Southern Hemisphere polar jet maintains an annular structure and does not shift directly over the ice sheet to deposit this dust.
Furthermore, regarding the position of the jet: the authors should reconsider the conceptual models of the jet stream presented in Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 6. Although some synoptic weather patterns can produce large meridional waves propagating toward (or even across) the North Pole, it seems implausible that a distinct polar jet stream from the Laptev Sea to Greenland would represent mean climatology. To inform these schematic depictions, we recommend examining mean wind climatologies from existing LGM climate model simulations (e.g., Brady et al., 2013), and perhaps also modern reanalysis products such as ERA5. Furthermore, the configuration of the polar and subtropical jet streams has large seasonality, and it could be beneficial to present both summer and winter circulation climatologies instead of annual.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We sincerely appreciate all reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive comments, which
greatly helped us to improve our manuscript. We provide a point-by-point response to each
comment below (responses are in orange).
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The paper by Kim et al. deals with the dust production and the routes of long-range transported
(LRT) dust be jet streams during the Late Pleistocene in the Northern Hemisphere. The study
reconstructed and compared the chemical properties of dust particles worldwide and from two
Yedoma sites with ice wedges in eastern Siberia (Batagay and Central Yakutia) by measuring
rare earth element (REE) abundances, strontium, neodymium, and oxygen isotope
compositions of inorganic substances.
The authors concluded that the Batagay and Central Yakutia samples have different
geochemical properties due to differences in local and LRT mechanisms. The Batagay ice
wedges show higher similarities to Chinese aeolian deposits and Greenland glacial dust while
the Central Yakutia ice wedges are more representative of local materials.
This is a valuable contribution to the international community. It can be published after major
revisions.
Thank you for the thorough summary, helpful comments and positive feedback to signify this
study.
1) First, it should be clarified what is loess (or loess-like sediments) in the Yedoma formations
and what is long-range transport (LRT) of dust. Both should have different grain sizes. The
loess-like deposits of the so-called Yedoma consist of silt-sized particles, but the LRT dust
contains mostly smaller particles. Quartz and also coarse grained sized particles may also be
local material or even recycled from older material in the area. The trapping of dust (and silt),
for example by vegetation or biocrusts is also an important factor in the development of loess
landscapes. Some of the material may have been temporarily deposited and then transported
again. There may also be some fluvial or colluvial input to the sections. However, some signals
in REE or Sr isotopes are obvious for LRT.
1-1. We agree that clearly distinguishing between loess (or loess-like sediments) and LRT dust
is essential. Yedoma consists predominantly of silt-sized particles deposited by mixed
sedimentary processes (e.g., aeolian, fluvial, and slope-derived input) during syngenetic ice
wedge growth. In contrast, LRT dust consists of finer particles (typically <10 or <5 μm)
transported long distances in the mid- to upper troposphere. Although Yedoma is generally silt-
dominated, our grain-size data show a secondary mode around 1 μm (Supplementary Fig. 4),
which we interpret as a fine-grained LRT component. These distinctions have been clarified in
the revised Introduction (Lines 48-50) and Results (Lines 93-95).
Coarser particles, including quartz, are plausibly derived from local recycling or short-range
transport, as you note. This interpretation is consistent with the isotope data, which vary
systematically with grain size. Sr-Nd isotope compositions suggest mixing between local and
LRT sources, while fine fractions (<10 and <5 μm) shift systematically toward OP-NMTP
values (Fig. 3). Oxygen isotope distributions of the <32 μm fraction broaden and show greater
overlap with the Chinese desert range, consistent with higher fine-grained LRT dust
contributions (Fig. 4).
Finally, we note that the relative prominence of LRT signals differs among proxies. REE
compositions tend to highlight LRT contributions more clearly, whereas Sr-Nd and O isotopes
reflect both local and LRT inputs but with stronger sensitivity to grain size and mineralogical
fractions. These differences likely account for the proxy-specific discrepancies observed, as
noted in Lines 175-179.
2) The chronological framework is very important for this study and its conclusions, and in my
opinion, this needs to be improved. The authors have separated pre- and late Glacial Maximum
for the Batagay and Yakutia ice wedges - but the chronological framework is quite uncertain,
and not described in detail. For example, Murton et al. (2022) show quite a lot of uncertainty
in the dating.
1-2. We appreciate your emphasis on the importance of the chronological framework. To
improve the age constraints of the Batagay ice wedges, we have considered additional
radiocarbon age data (Opel et al., under review; unpublished plant macro ages). These data
broadly suggest a formation interval between ~45,000 and 30,000 cal yr BP, corresponding to
middle to late MIS 3, but we have not formally incorporated them into the current manuscript
because they are not yet published. Instead, we rely on the established age range of ~60-27 ka
(late MIS 4 to MIS3; Murton et al., 2022), which substantially overlaps with MIS 3 (~57-29
ka). Accordingly, as clarified in the revised Introduction (Lines 71-76) and consistently adopted
throughout the revised text (e.g., Fig. 1; Discussion), we conservatively frame the Batagay ice
wedges within MIS 3. For clarity, we now assign the Batagay UIC to MIS 3 and the Central
Yakutia ice wedges to MIS 2.
3) There is a local ice cap on the Verkhoyansk Mountains between Batagay and Central Yakutia
that is out of phase with the global Last Glacial Maximum. This is also true for Pleistocene ice
extent in Alaska, see e.g. Stauch and Gualtier (1–3). They have a maximum extent in MIS 4 or
even just before. This shows that humidity is the main driver of ice and that local ice caps can
also influence at least the local wind fields.
In addition, there were so many climatic fluctuations during the last glacial cycle that this
should be clarified before drawing a big picture from the Chinese desert to Greenland based on
such a rough chronological framework. For example, the aforementioned LRT of dust from
China to Siberia needs to be proven and the period in which this direction occurred needs to be
established. Without a time frame, the conclusion remains highly speculative. Provide some
age constraints for your samples and also from the surround areas.
In my opinion, this should be also confirmed by paleoclimatic models. The North Atlantic and
the distribution of the Pleistocene ice influenced the jet stream. There are local wind fields over
the ice sheets, and there were easterly winds in front of the ice caps. There are quite a lot of
climatic fluctuations during the last glacial cycle and therefore quite a lot of fluctuations in the
direction of the jet stream. The Feno-Scandinavian ice sheet is important for the climate in Asia.
In particular, during the global Last Glacial Maximum, this ice sheet, at its largest extent,
blocked moist air masses to the east during its largest extent. There are eastly winds in front of
the ice sheet which are also responsible for the dust and loess distribution, please see the model
of Schaffernicht et al. (4), who also discussed the dust distribution in front of the European ice
sheet during the LGM. Local ice can also have an influence on wind direction and especially
on the transport of silt-size particles, as shown in many papers.
1-3. Thank you for these insightful suggestions. Your comments prompted us to focus more
closely on the climatic fluctuations during the last glacial cycle. We now conservatively
interpret the Batagay ice wedges as forming during MIS 3 (see response 1-2), a period
characterized by relatively warm and unstable climate conditions. We also fully agree that local
ice caps in the Verkhoyansk Mountains likely reached their maximum extent during MIS 4 or
earlier, driven by moisture availability, and did not expand significantly during the LGM.
The Verkhoyansk local ice cap appears to have remained limited even during MIS 3. Therefore,
there was probably little difference in its extent between MIS 3 (when the Batagay ice wedges
formed) and the LGM (when the Central Yakutia ice wedges formed). Based on this, we have
substantially revised our interpretation: rather than attributing changes in dust transport to ice-
sheet extent around Beringia, we now focus on the role of climate-driven variability in
synoptic-scale atmospheric circulation. As the Verkhoyansk ice cap was likely not
extensively developed during either MIS 3 or the LGM, a detailed discussion of its potential
influence on local wind fields would be overly speculative. We have therefore chosen not to
elaborate further on this point in the revised manuscript.
Our revised Discussion section highlights the possibility of ‘episodic meridional transport
of Asian dust to the Arctic across Siberia’, even under past climate conditions. This pathway
is supported by modern observations and modeling studies (Huang et al. 2015; Zhao et al.
2022), where cyclonic systems over northeast Asia facilitate rapid meridional transport.
We propose that such events were relatively frequent during MIS 3 (warmer and more variable
climate) compared to the LGM, thereby explaining the stronger Chinese dust signals in the
Batagay samples. In contrast, during the LGM, the development of the Siberian High and the
southward displacement of the westerlies (Brady et al., 2013; Yanase & Abe-Ouchi, 2007)
likely suppressed meridional transport, resulting in weaker Chinese dust signatures in Central
Yakutia. Although paleoclimatic modeling could further test this mechanism, such analysis lies
beyond the scope of this study. Instead, we believe that our findings will provide a valuable
geochemical basis for future model-based investigations of dust transport under paleoclimate
conditions.
4) Statistics:
The biplots in Figures 2 and 3 show only the overlap between the REE or isotope ratios of the
samples with those of the other proxies. In order to provide a more reliable distinction, a
statistical analysis with respect to the differences between samples and proxies can improve
the interpretation to which group the samples are assigned. Another aspect which to consider
is whether the samples and the data from the proxies are of the same age.
1-4 (1). Thank you for this constructive suggestion. We agree that statistical approaches can be
useful to summarize complex geochemical datasets. However, in our case we consider such
approaches less suitable for several reasons. First, our samples represent mixtures of both local
and distal sources rather than a single provenance. A simple statistical clustering against
reference datasets would therefore risk oversimplifying these multi-source signals and may not
appropriately capture the true provenance characteristics. Second, multivariate methods like
PCA emphasize the largest axes of variance and may obscure the more subtle but critical
features (e.g., Eu anomalies, grain-size independent tracers suggested by Ferrat et al., 2011)
that we highlight in our interpretation. To address your concern regarding the limited
confirmation in the original biplots, we have instead expanded our direct geochemical
comparisons by adding further element ratios (e.g., Eu/Eu*, Y/∑REE, Y/Tb) in Fig. 2 and a
series of new plots in Supplementary Fig. 6. In addition, Fig. 3 now includes further analyses
of the fine fractions and illustrates mixing relationships among multiple reference datasets as
an alternative to statistical analysis. We believe these additional visualizations more
appropriately capture the complex mixture of sources while avoiding the risk of
oversimplification inherent in broad statistical classifications.
With respect to the temporal comparability of samples and reference datasets, we note that
all ages are provided in Supplementary Data 2 and 3. Some reference materials are broadly
coeval with our samples (LGM or late Pleistocene), whereas others have either unknown ages
or substantially older formation ages. However, the proxies used in this study (REE, Sr-Nd,
and O isotopes) are not modified by surface processes and preserve the source composition, so
their use as provenance constraints does not require exact age equivalence. In the case of Sr-
Nd isotopes, while radiogenic decay can alter isotope ratios over geological time, we use the
present-day measured values of the reference samples rather than attempting to reconstruct
initial values. Nd isotopes, for instance, are reported as ε (0) indicating the present-day
Nd
measured values. This ensures that the direct comparisons remain valid for constraining
potential source contributions.
Figure 4 is not convincing and also on line 169 they mentioned an overlap. I think they should
test the differences.
1-4 (2). Fig. 4 presents grain-by-grain oxygen isotope data obtained by SIMS, displayed as
Gaussian kernel density curves to illustrate the internal variability of individual samples. By
contrast, the Chinese reference datasets are derived from bulk analyses. These reference
datasets cannot be represented as continuous distributions, as shown in Fig. 4, and direct
statistical comparison with our data is not feasible. Instead, we performed statistical tests
(Welch t-test, Mann-Whitney U, and permutation test) within our dataset to evaluate whether
oxygen isotope distributions differ statistically significantly among sites. The results, now
reported in the revised Fig. 4 caption and Methods, show that the Batagay sample is statistically
distinct from the Central Yakutia samples (p < 0.001), while no significant differences were
detected between the Cyuie and Churapcha samples (p ~ 0.8). In addition, to improve the
visibility of potential overlaps with the reference data, we have revised Fig. 4 by highlighting
the peak ranges where the reference values occur. This revision improves clarity in assessing
site-specific differences in the degree of overlap with reference values.
Some other questions remain open:
Is there any evidence to rule out repeated deposition and transport and a mixing of the sampled
material?
1-4 (3). We agree that repeated deposition, reworking, or mixing cannot be completely ruled
out. However, multiple observations suggest such processes are unlikely to dominate our
samples. First, we specifically targeted well-preserved syngenetic ice wedges without thaw-
related disturbance as noted in the Introduction (Lines 65-71; Lines 83-85; Kim et al., 2019;
Yang et al., 2023; Park et al., 2024). Unlike host sediments, the syngenetic ice wedge infill we
analyzed is less affected by redeposition or reworking. Second, our ice wedge samples formed
primarily by snow compaction and hoar frost accretion (Yang et al., 2023; Park et al., 2024),
rather than snowmelt or surface water infiltration, which minimizes the chance of secondary
input, providing a more direct record of atmospheric deposition during ice wedge growth
(Lines 81-83). Together, these features indicate that the geochemical signals we observe most
likely represent primary atmospheric deposition during ice wedge growth, rather than being
overprinted by repeated transport or mixing.
5) Figures:
I did not understand figure 1: is the legend for LGM, MIS 3 and MIS 4 for the extent of the
ice? If so, the figure is wrong. See my comments above, the ice in Siberia is related to the
incoming moisture from the west, which is blocked during MIS 4 and especially doing MIS 2.
The maximum extent in the interstadial of the last glacial cycle (MIS 3) in older literature is
based on radiocarbon ages and these are all minimum ages. The ice in eastern Siberia has its
maximum extent in MIS 4 or even earlier, because there is less moisture in that area afterwards
due to the blocking moist air masses by the Feno-Scandinavian ice sheet.
1-5. We agree that the Feno-Scandinavian Ice Sheet was extensive during MIS 4 and MIS 2,
and that its presence likely blocked incoming moisture, thereby limiting glaciation in eastern
Siberia during these periods. In our original Fig. 1, we referred to the ice sheet reconstructions
of Batchelor et al. (2019), which modelled ice extent at several time slices across MIS 3 (30,
35, 40, and 45 ka). Among these, only the 40 ka reconstruction shows more extensive ice cover
in eastern Siberia, due to the incorporation of the maximum Quaternary ice-extent template to
match the empirical evidence from the Kamchatka Peninsula. As you note, this 40 ka
configuration likely overestimates the ice extent for interior northeastern Siberia, including the
Verkhoyansk Mountains. To avoid potential misinterpretation, we have revised Fig. 1 by
excluding the 40 ka reconstruction and clarified this in the Methods section (Lines 408-414).
Instead, the ice extent for MIS 3 is now illustrated based on the other three time slices (30,
35, and 45 ka), which better reflect the likely limited glaciation in northeastern Siberia during this
period.
Frank Lehmkuhl, 6.3.2025

The Sm values of the Lena and Yana SPM samples seem to be incorrectly reported in

2-2. Thank you for this helpful suggestion. We have expanded our presentation of element
ratios by replacing several plots in Fig. 2 with ratios highlighted in Ferrat et al. (2011) (e.g.,
Eu/Eu*, Y/∑REE, Y/Tb). In addition, we have added a suite of new ratio plots in

Suggested improvements:
Fig. 3. The grain size fraction that each dataset represents would be good to include in the
figure, as the Sr isotopes can be influenced by the grain size. I would also like to hear what are

2-3. Thank you for the valuable comments. Regarding grain-size effects on Sr isotopes, we
conducted additional analyses of fine fractions (<10 and <5 μm). The grain-size fractions of all
samples and the compared datasets are now indicated in Fig. 3 and its caption, allowing
assessment of potential size-related effects. Regarding the Batagay values, we interpret their

and possibly MG. Although OP or EQLM appear as dominant sources based on REE
compositions (Fig. 2), they do not plot close to Batagay in the Sr-Nd isotopes (Fig. 3), as you
note. In the revised Fig. 3, however, mixing trajectories that combine OP and NMTP encompass
the Baagay data. We further note that REE and Sr-Nd isotopes are not necessarily controlled

discrepancy between the REE- and isotope-based provenance signals. This explanation has

While I do not disagree with the conclusions, the similarity of Greenlandic and Alaskan dust
