sediments, but rather treated as bounding constraints to define the plausible local compositional
range (Lines 164-166). These datasets allow us to approximate local endmember compositions
for comparison with our samples. Nevertheless, we agree that without more extensive
characterization of potential Beringian dust sources, it is not possible to fully distinguish local
versus LRT contributions in a quantitative sense. We have therefore interpreted our provenance
signals in qualitative rather than quantitative terms, emphasizing the consistent signatures
suggesting contributions from Chinese sources. We also highlight the need for future studies to
better characterize the geochemistry of potential local dust sources across Beringia, which will
be essential for refining source contributions in this region.
Further, we are not convinced that the sites, particularly Central Yakutia, are receiving dust
from Chinese deserts. If they were, we would expect to see compositions that reflect mixing of
local and long-range-transported (LRT) end-members. Instead, the Sr-Nd isotope compositions
of the sites are both tightly clustered, which is more indicative of input from a single source.
It’s possible that the Batagay samples follow a mixing trend between two end-members, with
one of them being Chinese desert material. However, the blue points in Fig. 3 really do not
appear to be following a mixing trend. Certainly if transport were occurring from Chinese
deserts over both sites and onward to Greenland, the data points should follow the same mixing
curve – which they clearly do not.
3-2. Thank you for this careful assessment. We agree that, in the simplest case of two-
component mixing with identical local endmembers and the Chinese LRT dust source, the data
would be expected to align along a single mixing trajectory. However, several factors make
such a pattern unlikely across both sites.
First, the two sites do not share a single local composition. In revised Fig. 3, the Central
Yakutia samples appear to be influenced predominantly by Aldan Shield-derived materials,
whereas Batagay may also integrate mafic inputs. Consequently, if Chinese possible source
areas (PSAs) contribute to both regions, each site would mix with a different local endmember,
resulting in distinct mixing trajectories rather than a single curve (Fig. 3b). In addition, because
the Chinese PSAs span a range of Sr-Nd values rather than a single point, it is more appropriate
to compare the samples against a mixing field rather than expect alignment along one idealized
line.
Second, the relative contributions of local versus LRT sources differ between the sites. The
tight clustering of bulk Central Yakutia samples reflects the dominance of locally derived
materials as you note, whereas Batagay compositions fall within the Chinese PSA-defined
mixing field (Fig. 3). Mixing trajectories between OP-NMTP and local endmembers
encompass the Batagay data, suggesting a local + LRT mixture. For Central Yakutia, bulk
samples remain close to the local field (Aldan Shield-like ɛ with radiogenic 87Sr/86Sr),
Nd
additional analyses of <10 μm and <5 μm fractions show a shift toward OP-NMTP
compositions. This shift, slightly higher ɛ values in addition to Sr isotope grain-size effects,
Nd
suggests the possibility of minor Chinese dust contributions to the fine fractions, even though
local sources remain dominant overall. Oxygen isotope data provide additional support (Fig.
4), where both samples show broadening of the <32 μm distributions and partial overlap with
Chinese desert values, yet the Central Yakutia samples retain a stronger local peak compared
to the Batagay samples.
Finally, we have removed speculative statements about a continuous Chinese-to-Greenland
pathway (see response 2-4 to reviewers #2). We now focus our interpretation on episodic
synoptic-scale meridional transport from China to East Siberia during MIS 3, and emphasize
that the Central Yakutia samples from the LGM contain a greater proportion of locally sourced
materials.
In addition, there are several important analytical details that are missing. One is the size
distribution of the Yedoma silts used for Sr-Nd analysis. Sr isotopes are known to have a grain
size effect (e.g. Biscaye and Dasch, 1971; Grousset and Biscaye, 2005; Gaiero, 2007); thus,
it is important to compare apples-to-apples size fractions among different studies. In the case of
LRT dust, scientists typically analyze the fine fraction (<5 um). At the very least, even if the
<5 um fraction was not isolated in this study, the measured grain size fraction used for the
isotope analyses needs to be stated. Based on Extended Data Fig. 5, it appears that the silts are
quite coarse (10s to 100s of µm diameter) – so isotopic analysis of the bulk size fraction is not
directly comparable to other fine-fraction data such as the dust from Greenland ice cores.
3-3. We fully acknowledge that Sr isotopes are sensitive to grain size, and that direct
comparison with other datasets requires clear specification of the analyzed size fractions.
Because of the limited availability of sample materials, our initial analyses were performed on
bulk aluminosilicates. To address this limitation and ensure comparability with fine-fraction
(<5 μm) datasets commonly used in LRT dust studies, we subsequently obtained additional
samples and conducted Sr-Nd isotope analyses on <10 μm and <5 μm fractions. The procedures
of size separation and analyses are now described in the revised Methods, and the grain-size
fractions of all datasets are clearly indicated in Fig. 3 and its caption.
The fine-fraction analyses show a marked shift in Sr isotopes consistent with the known
grain-size effect and a smaller shift in Nd isotopes relative to the bulk samples, both trending
toward the OP-NMTP endmembers. This pattern suggests not only the expected grain-size
effect of Sr isotope but also a relatively greater proportion of LRT dust in the finer fractions.
These additional measurements strengthen the robustness of our provenance interpretation and
ensure that our dataset is directly comparable with other fine-fraction studies.
The Sr and Nd isotopes were run with isotopic reference materials but it is unclear whether
they were used both as bracketing standards to correct the isotope ratios and as ‘unknowns’ to
assess accuracy of the analyses. Given the numbers analyzed for NBS-987 (n = 100) and JNdi-
1 (n = 140), it seems as though these are bracketing standards – in which case, additional
reference materials should be reported to provide an independent check on the accuracy of the
isotope ratios.
3-4. Bracketing standards were not used in our Sr and Nd isotope analyses. Instead, the
international reference materials NBS-987 (Sr) and JNdi-1 (Nd) were treated as unknowns to
assess external reproducibility and analytical accuracy. Instrumental mass bias was corrected
by internal normalization (86Sr/88Sr = 0.1194; 146Nd/144Nd = 0.7219). We clarify that the
numbers previously reported (n = 100 for NBS-987; n = 140 for JNdi-1) referred to the number
of measurement cycles within a single run, rather than replicate analyses, which may have
caused confusion. The originally reported values were based on one Sr standard run and two
Nd standard runs.
To better document reproducibility, we have revised the text to report long-term results based
on 15 replicate measurements of each standard during the measurement period, yielding
87Sr/86Sr = 0.710256 ± 6 (2σ, n = 15) and 143Nd/144Nd = 0.512122 ± 5 (2σ, n = 15). For
additional analyses of the fine fractions (<10 and <5 μm), 8 replicate measurements of each
standard yielded 87Sr/86Sr = 0.710252 ± 6 (2σ, n = 8) for NBS-987 and 143Nd/144Nd = 0.512119
± 4 (2σ, n = 8) for JNdi-1. These values are in good agreement with accepted values, confirming
the accuracy and reliability of our dataset. This information has been incorporated into the
revised Methods section.
In addition to source area geochemistry, the inference that Beringia was a source of high-
latitude dust in the past would be supported better through some mapped deposits of potential
source sediments. What is the geomorphic evidence for dust generation in this region? Are
there maps of glacial extent? Outwash plains?
3-5. We appreciate this thoughtful comment. In the original version, we speculated that
Beringia might have acted as a dust source during the Late Pleistocene, as numerical modeling
studies have suggested the plausibility of Siberia and Alaska as potential dust contributors
(Lambert et al., 2015; Mahowald et al., 2006). However, following the reviewers’ feedback,
we have removed this interpretation from the revised manuscript. We now focus on
distinguishing local versus LRT contributions recorded in the Batagay and Central Yakutia ice
wedges, without invoking Beringia as a separate dust source or transport pathway. Accordingly,
we no longer discuss geomorphic evidence for dust generation in Beringia.
The quartz O isotope data are interesting, in that several of the curves are bimodal, suggesting
inputs from multiple sources. The interpretation related to these data would be strengthened by
inclusion of comparable data on the potential source regions (e.g. Beringia and Asian deserts)
included in the figure, rather than just in the text. Ideally these would be plotted against another
provenance tracer (e.g. bivariate plot) and be supported by mixing calculations. The
interpretation provided on Line 175 – that both >32 and <32 sediments are contributed by LRT
of Chinese dust – is implausible. Considering that local sources can account for the oxygen
isotope values in the coarser fraction (Line 160), it does not make sense that all this relatively
coarse silt would have come thousands of km from China rather than from local sediments.
We think in this case, the most parsimonious interpretation needs to be made rather than basing
the interpretation on rare exceptions in the literature of long-distance coarse particle transport.
3-6. We have revised Fig. 4 and its caption to include oxygen isotope ranges of PSAs as colored
bands, allowing direct visual comparison. We also attempted bivariate plots and mixing
calculations, but their interpretive utility was limited because the available reference datasets
differ in sample type, number of samples, and grain-size fractions. These inconsistencies
preclude direct one-to-one comparisons across proxies. Nevertheless, the most pronounced
oxygen isotope compositions observed in the finest fractions of the Batagay samples fall within
the OP-NMTP range, consistent with other provenance tracers. This has been incorporated into
the revised Fig. 4.
As you note, attributing the coarse fractions to LRT from China was an over-interpretation.
We have therefore removed this statement from the manuscript. The ~15‰ peak in the coarse
fractions is interpreted as being most plausibly derived from local sediments, while
acknowledging that this peak range may still reflect a mixture of both local and LRT sources.
Likewise, the REE data in Extended Data Figure 4 are a helpful addition, but could be leveraged
toward the interpretation more effectively by including a panel that directly compares the
patterns of the different regions. We would advocate for further normalizing samples to a single
element, e.g. Yb or Lu, to more effectively compare the patterns. By eyeball, the data in panels
a and b actually look more similar to panel d than to panel c, supporting a local source for the
Yedoma silts. Figure 2 in the main text helps with these comparisons, but we are not convinced
that the Lena and Yana sediments fully characterize the local dust source region, given the
older bedrock to the south, shown in Extended Data Figure 1, which would provide sediment with
more negative εNd values, as shown by the Central Yakutia sites in Fig. 3.
3-7. We have revised Supplementary Fig. 5 by normalizing the datasets to Yb, which facilitates
clearer inter-comparisons of REE patterns as suggested. We also expanded local reference
datasets in revised Figs. 2-3 and Supplementary Figs. 5-6 to include Aldan Shield lamproites
and Kharaulakh-Suordakh volcanic rocks. Overall, the REE patterns in Supplementary Fig. 5
for both sites are loess-like, showing overall flat PAAS-normalized trends that differ from the
local bedrock compositions (Aldan Shield lamproites and Kharaulakh-Suordakh volcanic
rocks). However, the Central Yakutia samples exhibit pronounced Eu anomalies, a feature also
observed in the Lena and Yana SPM as well as in the local bedrocks. In the revised Fig. 2 and
Supplementary Fig. 6, the Lena SPM consistently resembles the Central Yakutia samples, but
also shows a shift toward Aldan Shield-like values. This combination suggests that the Central
Yakutia dust likely incorporates a contribution from Aldan Shield-derived material, which is
now noted in the revised text (Lines 115-119). As you note, the more negative ɛ values of the
Nd
Aldan Shield bedrock are consistent with the Central Yakutia compositions in revised Fig. 3.
Regarding the potential source regions shown on Fig. 3, the African sources are not relevant
based on geography and atmospheric transport patterns. We would recommend removing them
from the figure and discussion. In addition, the “Alaska” field reflects only the Fairbanks loess
data of Biscaye et al. 1997 and not more recent data from southcentral Alaska that characterize
the active Copper River dust source and related glaciofluvial sources (Koffman et al., 2022).
It may be worth including these data for a more complete representation of Alaska sources.
3-8. We have revised Fig. 3 and the associated discussion accordingly. As you note, African
source regions are geographically and climatologically implausible contributors to the studied
sediments. We have therefore removed the African sources from both the figure and the text to
avoid any misinterpretation. Regarding the Alaska field, we appreciate the suggestion to
incorporate additional datasets beyond the Fairbanks loess. We have updated Fig. 3 to include
more recent data from southcentral Alaska (Koffman et al., 2022). This revision provides a
more comprehensive representation of Alaskan sources.
Finally, while a Chinese desert source *could* be a plausible end-member for Batagay dust,
it does not follow that the jet itself had to have gone directly over the site. There is plenty of dust
transport that occurs not in the jet, for example through synoptic-scale systems. For instance,
extratropical cyclones transport dust from Patagonia to Antarctica, including onto the East
Antarctic plateau – yet the Southern Hemisphere polar jet maintains an annular structure and
does not shift directly over the ice sheet to deposit this dust.
3-9. Thank you for these helpful comments. We fully agree that the similarity between the
Chinese source data and our sample data does not necessarily imply that the polar jet stream
must have passed directly over our study sites. In light of this important point, we have revised
the Discussion to frame our interpretation in terms of broader atmospheric circulation related
to synoptic-scale systems, rather than the jet stream. In particular, modern observations show
that Asian dust can be transported meridionally to the Arctic via cyclonic systems over
northeast Asia (Huang et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2022), a mechanism conceptually similar to the
Patagonian dust transport to Antarctica, as noted in your comment. We now emphasize such
synoptic-scale variability as the more plausible driver of episodic long-range dust transport
during MIS 3, consistent with the strong Chinese dust signals observed in the Batagay samples.
This revision is reflected throughout the manuscript.
Furthermore, regarding the position of the jet: the authors should reconsider the conceptual
models of the jet stream presented in Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 6. Although some synoptic
weather patterns can produce large meridional waves propagating toward (or even across) the
North Pole, it seems implausible that a distinct polar jet stream from the Laptev Sea to
Greenland would represent mean climatology. To inform these schematic depictions, we
recommend examining mean wind climatologies from existing LGM climate model
simulations (e.g., Brady et al., 2013), and perhaps also modern reanalysis products such as
ERA5. Furthermore, the configuration of the polar and subtropical jet streams has large
seasonality, and it could be beneficial to present both summer and winter circulation
climatologies instead of annual.
3-10. We agree that our original schematic depictions of the jet stream may have given the
impression of representing mean climatology, which was not our intent. In the revised
manuscript, we have substantially simplified these figures and reframed them to illustrate
generalized dust transport pathways rather than specific jet stream tracks. In particular, the
meridional transport is not intended to represent mean circulation, but instead schematically
illustrates episodic events that were likely more ‘frequent’ during MIS 3 than during the LGM.
This is clarified in the revised Fig. 1 caption (Lines 583-585) and avoids potential
overinterpretation of the schematics as mean flow patterns.
While we recognize the significance of mean wind climatology from LGM simulations and
modern reanalysis products such as ERA5, a full model-data comparison lies beyond the scope
of this study. Instead, we draw on modern observational and modeling evidence (e.g., Huang
et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2022) to highlight how synoptic-scale variability can facilitate
meridional dust transport to the Arctic. We also acknowledge the importance of seasonality in
atmospheric circulation. However, given the temporal resolution of our samples, we cannot
resolve seasonal differences. We therefore retain a simplified depiction of dust transport events,
while clarifying this limitation in the revised Discussion (Lines 260-261).
